title: Accessibility and inclusive design
definition: People with different abilities, devices, connections, languages and levels of experience can complete the product's tasks. Accessibility is a baseline requirement and outranks brand expression.
intended_outcome: Primary tasks can be completed with a keyboard alone, with a screen reader, with zoom and with reduced motion; text contrast is sufficient in every theme; language is plain.
implementation_guidance: Target WCAG 2.2 level AA for every product screen. Text contrast is at least 4.5:1 (3:1 for large text) in every theme, evaluated on the actual background tokens.
All functionality works by keyboard with visible focus and a logical order. No keyboard traps.
Use semantic HTML and real labels first, ARIA only to fill gaps, and announce dynamic changes.
Respect prefers-reduced-motion. Never carry information by colour alone.
Support narrow viewports and 200 percent zoom without loss of content, and size touch targets for fingers.
Use plain language and locale-aware formats.
An accessibility defect is a finding that cannot be traded against a brand rule (the precedence rule, ADR-0021).

automated: Automated accessibility checks in the product CI (contrast computed from tokens, rule-based DOM checks), with results recorded.
Keyboard-only end-to-end tests of primary tasks.
expert_review: Manual screen-reader pass over the primary tasks.
customer_feedback: Feedback from users with access needs, with their consent.

limitations: Automated tools detect only part of the issues WCAG covers.
Meeting WCAG is not a claim that the product works for all disabled users.
The engine cannot certify legal accessibility compliance.

evidence.summary: Normative success criteria for accessible web content. Supports the guidance items (contrast, keyboard, focus, target size); says nothing about commercial effect.
evidence.citation: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (w3.org/TR/WCAG22/).

evidence.summary: The owner directs that the brand framework must never override accessibility.
